analysis.one_liner: Requires child-resistant compartments, warning labels, and packaging for small coin batteries children can swallow.
analysis.headline: Reese's Law cleared the Senate Commerce Committee with bipartisan support on December 14, 2022, but the full Senate never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a safety standard for small "button cell" or coin batteries, like those in remotes, key fobs, and singing cards, which children sometimes swallow with fatal results. Products using these batteries would need battery compartments young children cannot open, plus prominent warning labels, and batteries sold separately would have to come in child-resistant packaging. The bill passed a Senate committee but never reached a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and caregivers of small children, who would face fewer swallowable batteries in reach; and consumers generally, who would get clearer warnings that a swallowed battery is a medical emergency. Toy and household products with coin batteries would be redesigned so children six and under cannot get into the compartment, and loose batteries would ship in child-resistant packages.

how_it_helps.text: Products containing button cell or coin batteries would have to meet a performance standard securing the battery compartment so children six or younger cannot access the battery, and would carry warning labels on the packaging, in the manual, and on the product where practicable.

Button cell or coin batteries sold separately or included separately with a product would have to be packaged in child-resistant packaging under the same standards used for other dangerous household substances, effective 180 days after enactment.

Warning labels would have to clearly identify the ingestion hazard and tell consumers to keep new and used batteries away from children and to seek immediate medical attention if a battery is swallowed.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and importers of button cell batteries and of the many consumer products that use them would bear the cost of redesigning battery compartments, testing products, printing warning labels, and switching to child-resistant packaging. Those costs would largely be passed through to consumers in prices, though the bill applies only to products manufactured or imported after the standards take effect.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on battery and product makers and would be passed on to consumers in slightly higher prices, and the bill exempts toys that already meet the battery accessibility and labeling rules in existing federal toy regulations, as well as batteries meeting an industry (ANSI) lithium battery standard, narrowing what the new rules cover.

The bill lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission rely on a voluntary industry standard in place of writing its own mandatory rule, which supporters of stronger regulation generally see as a weaker path because industry-written standards can lag or fall short.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is protection of young children from a hazard that can be fatal within hours and is hard for parents to detect; the costs are one-time design and packaging changes spread across many inexpensive consumer products. The exemptions and the voluntary-standard pathway slightly dilute the bill, but the core mandate — secured battery compartments and child-resistant packaging — directly addresses the hazard at modest cost.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill in December 2022 and put it on the Senate's calendar of business, but the Senate never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced Reese's Law on November 30, 2021, joined from the start by Senators Blackburn (R-TN), Markey (D-MA), Luján (D-NM), and Durbin (D-IL); the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.
On May 11, 2022, the Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, but it sat unreported for another seven months.

On December 14, 2022 — twenty days before the Congress ended — the committee, chaired by Senator Cantwell, formally reported the bill and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, the waiting list for bills eligible for floor consideration.
The Senate never voted on the bill, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and importers of button cell batteries and the products that use them are better off, at least for that Congress, because no federal law required child-resistant compartments and packaging; nothing in the record shows organized opposition, so timing and the end of the session appear to have mattered more than any opponent.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from the day it was introduced — 3 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 50 Senate Republicans as cosponsors — and cleared the Commerce Committee favorably; there were no recorded floor votes showing a partisan split.

industries.industry: Button cell and coin battery makers
industries.note: Batteries sold loose or included with products would need child-resistant packaging and hazard warning labels, a real but modest cost. The bill also exempts lithium batteries meeting the industry's own ANSI C18.3M marking and packaging standard, so some product lines would face no new requirement.

industries.industry: Consumer electronics and household product makers
industries.note: Any product designed to use a coin battery — remotes, key fobs, greeting cards, watches — would need a child-resistant battery compartment and labels on packaging, manuals, and where practicable the product itself. The industry's interest in avoiding redesign and testing costs runs against the child-safety requirement.

Toys already complying with the battery accessibility and labeling requirements of existing federal toy safety regulations (16 CFR part 1250) are exempt from the new standards, sparing the toy industry the cost its product category might otherwise have faced.
